newsitem.title: USA: Tandy downsizing a sign of hard times.
newsitem.headline: Tandy downsizing a sign of hard times.

text.p: Tandy Corp's decision to shut its chain of Incredible Universe superstores is a reflection of tough times in the consumer electronics sector but also a logical end to an ill-conceived experiment, analysts said.

Tandy said on Monday it would sell all 17 Incredible Universe stores and also shut 19 of its 108 Computer City stores in North America. Company officials said stiff competition had taken its toll on the enormous stores which offered the full range of consumer electronic goods.
Analysts said the news was the latest in a string of clear signals that consumer demand for personal computers has slowed sharply in recent months, and might not recover quickly.

"From the individual consumer point of view, I would think the earliest we are likely to see a turn would be the second half of 1997, and that would only be if we do not have a recession," said Ursula Moran, an analyst with Sanford C. Bernstein & Co in New York.

"There will of course be PCs sold between now and the second half of 1997. The problem is they will be sold under a fair amount of duress for retailers with extraordinarily aggressive promotions and price-cutting," Moran said.

She and other analysts said the market penetration of personal computers was already very high among affluent social groups and that growth in the market of computers for first-time buyers was limited as new customers were less well off than the first waves of customers.
A scarcity of exciting new products to compare with the heady days that surrounded the launch of Microsoft's "Windows 95" software was also limiting computer upgrades for individuals and households.
Consequently, intense market competition had pushed down profit margins and forced up advertising costs just as many retailers opened stores and sharply expanded their selling space.
Best Buy Co Inc., one of the country's largest retailers of electronics, PCs and appliances, earlier this month reported its first quarterly loss in over a decade.
Analysts said Tandy's decision to abandon Incredible Universe allowed it to focus on expanding its strong chain of Radio Shack stores, but that market conditions remained tough.
"The problem is in consumer electronics. There is a lot of competition and that is hurting profitability," said Peter Caruso, an analyst at Merill Lynch.
And most industry experts said that, aside from the generalized industry-wide problems, Tandy made serious errors in its management of the Incredible Universe chain.
"It was a flawed concept from the outset and, as the industry got more competitive, it was not surprising they were unable to turn a profit," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
He and others said the Incredible Universe stores, which were each about 180,000 square feet, were too large and cumbersome and were particularly vulnerable to a slowdown in consumer retail sales.
Apart from the slowdown in personal computer sales, 1996 had also been a disappointing year for audio and many television products, analysts said.

But investors reacted calmly to Tandy's restructuring announcement, which was widely expected. The company's shares ended 3/4 higher at 46-1/4, CompUSA shares gained 1/2 to 20-1/2 and Circuit City Stores Inc added 1/4 to close at 29-7/8.
